html:
City walls about 19 km long around Rome, built from 271 to 275 under the emperor Aurelian. For centuries Rome had grown without a wall, protected by armies on distant frontiers. In the third-century crisis Germanic raiders reached northern Italy, and the capital needed defending again.

The walls were brick-faced concrete with a square tower every 30 m or so. They enclosed the seven hills, the Campus Martius and Trastevere across the Tiber, far more than the old Servian Wall. Later rulers raised them, especially around 400 as the Goths threatened.

They did not stop every attack; the Visigoths entered in 410 and the Vandals in 455. They stayed Rome's defence until 1870, when Italian troops breached them at Porta Pia to take the city. Large stretches and many gates still stand.
